notes.TorusEuler.auxiliaryLemma12: The formal theorem chooses an exponent parameter, a nondecreasing threshold $\mathcal B$, and $N_1$ such that every initial frequency $N\ge N_1$ admits a selected common construction with $\lambda_0=N$. In that one construction, every fixed pair $(m,q)$ eventually satisfies $\|\partial_t^q(U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j)\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$ throughout $[0,S_j]$, and the differentiated correction is continuous in that spatial norm. The starting stage may depend on both orders and the construction. This is a proved selected-construction version of auxiliary Lemma 1.2. It does not quantify over all cutoff symbols, all admissible thresholds or all constructions having the Section 7 conclusions. The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm is $\sum_{i\le m}(\sup|D^if|+[D^if]_{1/2})$, where $D^if$ is the full $i$th derivative tensor in operator norm.
notes.TorusEuler.auxiliaryLemma13: The formal theorem chooses an exponent parameter, a nondecreasing threshold and an initial-frequency lower bound before constructing the sequence. Every sufficiently large initial frequency then admits a selected construction in which each $q$ has an integer $\psi_q$ and a starting stage such that $|\partial_t^iU_j|\le\lambda_j^{\psi_q}$ and $|\partial_t^iR_j|\le\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}$ for all $i\le q$ and all later stages. Both time curves are continuous in the spatial supremum norm on $[0,S_j]$. This proves the stated time estimates with a more specific, nonnegative integer exponent. It is existential in the selected construction and does not prove the separate generalized assertion for every qualifying construction.
notes.TorusEuler.auxiliaryTerminalSmoothness: The formal statement chooses an integer $b$, a nondecreasing threshold $\mathcal B$ and $N_1$ before $N$. For every $N\ge N_1$ it supplies stages with $\lambda_0=N$, the eventual time and mixed correction estimates, and activation times tending to a finite $T>0$ below every stage endpoint. It also supplies an odd smooth maximal periodic Euler solution on $[0,T)$ with bounded velocity, central vorticity tending to infinity, and infinite time integrals of gradient and vorticity supremum norms. Both velocity and its first time derivative have all local spatial derivative limits off the torus origin. The velocity extends periodically and smoothly to all real times off that point; Euler is not imposed after $T$. The exported conclusion does not state $U_j\to u$, although the supplied assembly proof constructs and uses that limit. It selects one threshold, rather than treating every admissible threshold.
notes.TorusEuler.centeredCell: The formal domain is the closed cube $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:-1/2\le x_i\le1/2\text{ for }i=1,2,3\}$. Lebesgue integration over this cube defines the pressure normalization and the torus essential-supremum norms. The cube itself does not identify opposite faces; that identification is represented by imposing integer-translation invariance on the fields. Both boundary faces are included, but they have zero three-dimensional measure and therefore do not change these integrals or essential suprema. This is precisely the fundamental-cell convention in the introduction, not an additional boundary condition of vanishing velocity.
notes.TorusEuler.child_flow_scaled_gradient_le: Let $\mathsf D,\lambda\ge1$, let $a,c$ be nonnegative integers, and suppose $\ell_*^{-1}\le\mathsf D^a$ and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$. If nonnegative quantities $A,B$ satisfy $A,B\le K\mathsf D^c\lambda^{-5/4}$, then $\ell_*^{-1}A+h^{-1}B\le2K\mathsf D^{a+c}\lambda^{-3/4}$. In Lemma 5.10 these quantities bound derivatives of the label velocity and its longitudinal component. The theorem is a scalar inequality: it does not prove the input derivative estimates or identify the left side with the actual gradient. Positivity of the physical radius is imposed elsewhere; the formal inequality only needs the displayed reciprocal bound.
notes.TorusEuler.child_flow_scaled_gradient_sm: Let $\mathsf D,\lambda\ge1$, $C,\delta\ge0$, and nonnegative integer exponents $p\le b$. Suppose $C\le\delta\Gamma_P$, $\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, and a quantity $G$ satisfies $G\le C\mathsf D^p\lambda^{-3/4}$. Then $G\le\delta$. This is the numerical absorption used before the Gronwall estimate in Lemma 5.10. It applies once $G$ has been identified with a bound for the scaled gradient; no differentiability or flow assertion is part of this lemma. The weaker frequency exponent $-1/12$ is sufficient because $\lambda\ge1$.
notes.TorusEuler.complexFrozenSymbols_fiveJets: Let $r(\xi)$ be a smooth family of orthogonal projections on an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$, and let $B$ be a bounded operator on a real Hilbert space with a compatible complexification. Assume $\langle Bw,w\rangle\ge\mu\|w\|^2$, $\mu>0$, whenever $r(\xi)w=w$. At a point $\xi$ suppose $\|D^ir(\xi)\|\le D^i$ for $0\le i\le5$, with $D\ge1$. Put $Q=2+\mu^{-1}+\|B\|$ and $C=(5!)^2(2D)^5$. The derivatives through order five of the complexified inverse of $rBr+I-r$ are bounded by $CQ^{11}$; for its composition with $r$ the bound is $32D^5CQ^{11}$. No nonzero-frequency hypothesis is imposed in this abstract statement. The application in Appendix A.1 uses nonzero frequencies, where the Leray symbol is smooth.
notes.TorusEuler.complexifiedHalfHolderFourier: Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space, $B:H\to H$ bounded linear, and $v\in C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;H)$. For every spatial frequency $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, the formal statement gives $\widehat{Bv}(n)=B_{\mathbb C}\widehat v(n)$, where $B_{\mathbb C}$ is the extension of $B$ to the compatible complex space used for Fourier coefficients. The coefficient $B$ is independent of the spatial label. This includes $H=L^2([0,1];\mathbb R^3)$: $B$ may act on whole time paths while preserving each spatial Fourier mode. This establishes coefficient diagonalization after freezing. It does not identify the projection's symbol, invert a projected equation, or require coercivity.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_angularLeray: The map $\xi\mapsto I-\widehat\xi\otimes\widehat\xi$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, and hence on the unit sphere used in Appendix A.1. The formal statement permits every differentiability order there. It makes no continuity or differentiability assertion at zero, where the symbol is separately defined to be the identity. This establishes the spatial part of the projection-symbol regularity; the projection on $L^2$ time paths also involves subtraction of the time mean.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_endpointFixedInver: Let $S(t)$ be a family of bounded linear isomorphisms of a real Banach space, whose forward operators vary with $C^n$ regularity on a prescribed set of times. Then $S(t)^{-1}$ varies with the same regularity in operator norm; $n$ may be finite or infinite. On a closed interval this uses derivatives from within that interval. Appendix A.2 applies the result after establishing invertibility of $S(t)v=\mathbb P(K(t)v)$ in a spatial norm. It neither proves that inverse exists nor supplies its coercivity estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_endpointPrimitive_: If $T>0$ and $f:[0,T]\to E$ is $C^n$ in a real Banach space, for an integer $n\ge0$, then $Jf(t)=\int_0^tf(s)\,ds$ is $C^{n+1}$ on $[0,T]$. Differentiability at the endpoints is one-sided, so no smooth extension beyond the interval is required. In Appendix A.2 this applies to $f=\Omega v$ in a chosen spatial norm. It supplies the gain in time regularity; smoothness in space must be established independently.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_endpointVelocity_a: Let $T>0$, let $S(t)$ be smooth bounded isomorphisms of a real Banach space $X$, and let $P:E\to X$ be bounded linear. Assume $\Omega(t):X\to E$ and $L(t)\in E$ are smooth, $c\in X$ is constant, and continuous $v$ satisfies $S(t)v(t)=c+P J(\Omega v)(t)-P L(t)$ on $[0,T]$. Then $v$ and $Jv$ are smooth in time. This is the time bootstrap in Appendix A.2, applied after choosing a spatial norm. It does not by itself give spatial derivatives or pressure regularity. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiffOn_flatActivation_smu: Let $a<b$, let $\chi$ be a globally smooth real function with $\chi(t)=0$ for every $t\le a$, and let $g(t,x)$ be smooth on $[a,b]\times V$, with values in a normed space. The formal statement proves that $\chi(t)g(t,x)$ is smooth on $(-\infty,b]\times V$. Although $g$ is defined at earlier times, no regularity there is assumed: multiplication by zero removes those values. This supplies a gluing principle for the products after (3.7). The paper gives its cutoff only on $[0,T]$; this particular result requires a globally smooth extension of it.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiff_localizedTransported: Fix a time, a differentiability order $m$, and a map $A$. Suppose $A$ and the evaluated label field $a\mapsto f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$ are $C^m$. Assume $0<\delta\le1/2$ and that this field vanishes whenever some coordinate satisfies $|a_i|>1/2-\delta$. Extending it periodically from the centered cell and composing with $A$ gives a $C^m$ field; the result includes $m=\infty$. The formal result imposes no lattice condition on $k_*\in\mathbb R^3$. The zero collar is the reason arbitrary phases can be extended without seams; periodicity of the resulting Eulerian field additionally requires the inverse map to commute with integer translations.
notes.TorusEuler.contDiff_waveSwitch: Let $\theta:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$ be the fixed smooth transition, equal to zero for arguments at most zero and one for arguments at least one. For any real activation time $t_0$ and rate $r$, the formal statement proves that $\widetilde\chi(t)=\theta(r(t-t_0))$ is smooth on $\mathbb R$. In particular there is no loss of regularity at the activation time or at the end of the switching interval. This conclusion does not require $r>0$. That positivity is needed separately to interpret the transition as switching on as time increases.
notes.TorusEuler.continuousOn_endpointFixedInv: Let $X$ be a real Banach space and let $S(t):X\to X$ be bounded linear isomorphisms for every real $t$. If their forward operators vary continuously in operator norm on a prescribed set $I$, then their inverses vary continuously in operator norm on $I$. No common bound on the inverse norms is a hypothesis of this statement. In Appendix A.2, take $I=[0,1]$ and $S(t)v=\mathbb P(K(t)v)$ on divergence-free $C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3)$ fields. The fixed-time inverse must first be constructed, and continuity of the forward family must be established; the theorem then supplies continuity of the inverse family.
notes.TorusEuler.continuous_and_norm_sub_le_en: Let $w$ be a spatially half-Hölder field with values in $L^2([0,T];E)$. Its primitive $Jw(t)$ is continuous in the spatial $C^{0,1/2}$ norm and satisfies $\|Jw(t)-Jw(s)\|_{C^{0,1/2}}\le|t-s|^{1/2}\|w\|_{C^{0,1/2}(L^2)}$ for $s,t\in[0,T]$. The half-Hölder norm is the maximum of supremum and seminorm. The formal statement allows an arbitrary metric label space, including the unit torus. Applied to $w=\Omega v$, this makes the right side of (A.9) continuous before continuity of $v$ has been recovered. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.coordinateCurl_rankOne: Let $\mathbf a,\kappa\in\mathbb R^3$ and let $D$ be the linear map $v\mapsto(\kappa\cdot v)\mathbf a$, the convention for $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$. Forming the coordinate curl from this derivative matrix gives $\kappa\times\mathbf a$, with the usual orientation of the coordinate basis. No differentiability assertion about a velocity is needed for this algebraic identity; no orthogonality or nonzero-vector assumptions are required. When $D$ is a contribution to $\nabla U_j(t,0)$, the identity gives exactly the contribution to vorticity used in Proposition 8.2. It fixes both the tensor order and the cross-product sign.
notes.TorusEuler.couplingRatioOfGain_step: Let $L>0$ and $L_+\ge640L$, and set $\varepsilon=L^{-2}$ and $\varepsilon_+=L_+^{-2}$. The formal statement gives $\varepsilon_+=(L/L_+)^2\varepsilon\le\varepsilon/32$, together with $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}=LL_+\le L_+^2$. For step $j$, take $L=L_j$ and $L_+=L_{j+1}$; then these are the ratio estimate (7.9) and the following comparison of crossing times. Both gains and both ratios are positive under the hypotheses, so inverse squares and the negative half-power have their ordinary meanings. The statement assumes the gain separation; it does not prove it from the frequency recurrence.
notes.TorusEuler.crossingClock_le_endpointHalf: Suppose $\mu,c,L>0$, $L_+\ge640L$, $r\ge c\mu^{1/8}$ and $L_+\ge2/c$. Define $\varepsilon=L^{-2}$, $\varepsilon_+=L_+^{-2}$ and $\tau=\mu^{-1/8}L_+^3$. The formal theorem proves $2(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}/r\le\tau$. With $L=L_j$ and $L_+=L_{j+1}$, the left side is the physical duration corresponding to the upper end of the crossing bracket, while $\tau=\tau_j$. This places any crossing already known to lie in that bracket before $t_j+\tau_j$. The theorem neither constructs a crossing nor states the intermediate bound by a constant times $\mu^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^2$.

notes.TorusEuler.cutoffSchwartzKernel: Let $\psi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and vanish for $|\zeta|>2$. The formal object is the complex-valued Schwartz function $K=\check\psi$, using the Fourier convention compatible with the modes $e^{2\pi i\xi\cdot x}$. Smoothness and the support condition give rapid decay of every derivative. No plateau, sign or evenness assumption is needed to define this kernel. In particular, the definition alone does not give integral one: its integral is $\psi(0)$, and the paper's condition $\psi=1$ near zero supplies that value. The operator representation and vanishing moments are separate results.
notes.TorusEuler.derivWithin_kineticForm_sub_v: Let $F(t)$ be a bounded operator on a real Hilbert space, differentiable at the time considered, with $F_t=MF$. Set $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. Then $K_t-\Omega=2F^TF_t$. This is the second identity in (4.2), expressed for arbitrary operators rather than only a particle-flow derivative. The time set must determine derivatives uniquely; a nondegenerate closed interval does, using its one-sided derivatives at endpoints. No symmetry of $M$, invertibility of $F$, or Euler equation is assumed.
notes.TorusEuler.deriv_waveProfile_bounds: For every $0<h\le1$ and every real phase $s$, the selected profile satisfies $-h/2\le F_h'(s)\le1$. The profile is built from a periodized narrow bump after subtracting its mean and normalizing the slope at zero. This formal estimate supplies (1.10) with the explicit constant $C=1/2$ in place of an unspecified absolute constant. It controls the negative part of the slope, which produces positive pressure curvature when the pressure coefficient is nonnegative. It does not bound the absolute slope by a multiple of $h$; in fact $F_h'(0)=1$.
notes.TorusEuler.divergence: For a differentiable vector field $v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, the formal definition gives $\operatorname{div}v(x)=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_i v_i(x)$ by applying $D_xv$ to the coordinate vectors and summing the diagonal entries. This agrees with the paper’s convention $(\nabla v)_{ij}=\partial_jv_i$. The derivative expression is defined even at a point where $v$ is not differentiable, with value zero there; consequently the equation $\operatorname{div}v=0$ alone does not imply classical incompressibility without regularity assumptions. The Euler-solution condition supplies smoothness. The present definition concerns vector fields; the rowwise divergence of a matrix field is not itself defined by this declaration.

For a twice continuously differentiable vector field $u:\mathbb R^3	o\mathbb R^3$ with $\operatorname{div}u=0$ everywhere, $\operatorname{div}((u\cdot
abla)u)=\operatorname{tr}((
abla u)^2)$ at every point. The square is matrix composition, not the sum of the squared entries of $
abla u$. This identity follows by differentiating the product and using $u\cdot
abla\operatorname{div}u=0$. It is the spatial identity used in §5.7 to choose $\Delta p=-\operatorname{tr}((
abla u)^2)$ so that the momentum residual is divergence free. The result assumes neither periodicity nor a time-dependent Euler equation.
notes.TorusEuler.divergence_affineWaveVelocity: At a fixed time and point, assume only that the scalar profile $F$ is differentiable at $k\cdot x$. The formal identity for $u(x)=Dx+F(k\cdot x)\mathbf a$ is $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{tr}D+F'(k\cdot x)(k\cdot\mathbf a)$. This gives the intermediate divergence formula in the proof of Lemma 2.1. It does not assert the final zero there: one must additionally impose $\operatorname{tr}D=0$ and $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$. No time evolution equation or smoothness away from the evaluated phase is needed for this spatial calculation.
notes.TorusEuler.divergence_completedWaveOn:
Fix a time and an open spatial region. Suppose the inverse label map is $C^2$ there, its transported covector agrees with $(D_xA)^Tk_*$ and never vanishes, and the continuous phase profile is perpendicular to that covector. Assume the associated potential is jointly $C^2$ in label and phase near every evaluated point. Then the formal statement proves $
abla_x\cdot(V^
atural+C[V]^
atural)=0$ throughout the region. The completed field is the curl of the transported potential. This is the local cancellation used for $V_2+C_3$ in §1.3; constructing a smooth periodic field on the whole torus requires the additional extension argument.
notes.TorusEuler.divergence_curl: Let $Q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be twice continuously differentiable at $x$. The formal statement is $\nabla\cdot(\nabla\times Q)(x)=0$, using ordinary Euclidean spatial derivatives. Equality of the mixed second derivatives gives the cancellation. This is the differential identity behind the divergence-free completed wave in §3.1. No periodicity, compact support or parent flow is assumed. To apply it to the transported potential, one must first establish its $C^2$ regularity; the definition of a curl on an arbitrary function alone does not provide that hypothesis.
notes.TorusEuler.divergence_gradient_cutoffPre:
Let $V$ be $C^2$ and divergence free, let $p,\Pi$ be $C^2$, and suppose $\Delta p=-\operatorname{tr}((
abla u)^2)$ and $W+(V\cdot

abla\Pi=R$. At the point considered, require $W$ differentiable and $\operatorname{div}W=0$. Then $\Delta(p-\Pi)=-\operatorname{tr}((
abla u)^2-(
abla V)^2)-\operatorname{div}R$. In §5.7, $W=V_t$, $R=R_V$, and writing $v_\Lambda=u-V$ expands the trace difference into the paper’s two cross terms. This identity does not require periodicity. The term $-\operatorname{div}R_V$ is essential because $\Pi$ is the pressure of an approximate solution.
notes.TorusEuler.divergence_piola_of_contDiffA: Let $X$ be $C^2$ near a label $a$, let $Y$ be a differentiable local inverse near $X(a)$, and suppose $\det DX=1$ near $a$. For a vector field $v$ differentiable at $a$, the pushed-forward field $b(x)=DX(Y(x))v(Y(x))$ satisfies $\operatorname{div}b(X(a))=\operatorname{div}v(a)$. This is the Piola identity used for (4.12). The formal result is local and does not require an entire particle flow. When $X$ is the incompressible parent flow, it transfers the label velocity's zero divergence to the physical correction.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointClosedTimeNorm: For a normed-space-valued function $f$, the expression takes the real supremum of $\{\|f(t)\|:0\le t\le T\}$. In the endpoint theorems the underlying norm is the spatial half-Hölder norm, giving $\|f\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}}$. The formal convention assigns zero if this set is empty or unbounded above; it is not an infinite norm in those cases. In (A.3) and Theorem 4.2, positive compact intervals and continuous curves ensure a nonempty bounded set, so the value is the ordinary finite supremum. The definition alone imposes neither condition.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointDisplacementEnergy_co: Let $T\ge0$, let $\xi$ be a continuously differentiable path in a real Hilbert space with $\xi(T)=0$, and let $H(t)$ be continuous with $\langle H(t)w,w\rangle\le\|w\|^2$. The formal statement gives $\int_0^T(\|\xi_t\|^2-\langle H\xi,\xi\rangle)\,dt\ge(1-T^2/2)\int_0^T\|\xi_t\|^2\,dt$. It needs neither $\xi(0)=0$ nor symmetry of $H$. The factor is at least $1/2$ when $T\le1$; positivity is not claimed for arbitrary $T$. This is a one-path estimate underlying (1.9). The paper's displayed $L^2_{t,a}$ estimate additionally integrates over particle labels.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointHessian: Given bounded operators $M$ and $N$ on a real Hilbert space, define $H=-(N+M^2)$. The intended application is $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$ and $N=M_t$, yielding $H^\#$ in (4.1). The expression itself does not assert that $N$ is a derivative, that $M$ comes from a velocity, or that $H$ is symmetric. Those interpretations and the inequality $H\le I$ must be supplied separately. This distinction permits the same energy algebra for parents with nonzero Euler residual.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointHessian_eq_pressureHe:
Let $0<T$, $t\in[0,T]$, and let $U$ be jointly $C^2$ on the closed slab. Suppose $X_t=U(t,X)$ at the time considered and $
abla p(t,\cdot)$ is differentiable at $X(t)$. With $M=D_xU(t,X(t))$ and $R_U=U_t+(U\cdot
abla)U+
abla p$, the formal statement proves $-(M_t+M^2)=(D_x^2p-D_xR_U)(t,X(t))$. Time derivatives at endpoints are taken within $[0,T]$. This is the identity used in §1.2 to treat approximate parents. No incompressibility or exact Euler equation is assumed, and the effective Hessian need not be symmetric when the residual is nonzero.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointJointSpatialProjectio: For $T>0$, consider square-integrable vector fields on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^3$. Orthogonal projection onto spatially divergence-free fields commutes with $\mathcal Qv=v-T^{-1}\int_0^Tv(s)\,ds$. Thus their composition projects onto fields satisfying both constraints. This justifies $\mathcal R=\mathbb P\mathcal Q$ in Appendix A; the paper uses the special case $T=1$. The assertion is in the space-time $L^2$ space, where fields that agree almost everywhere represent the same field. Hölder-space versions require their separate compatibility results.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy: For $T\ge0$ and continuous operator fields $F,M$ on $[0,T]$, put $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. For $v\in L^2([0,T];E)$, the defined energy is $\|Fv\|_{L^2}^2+\langle\Omega v,Jv\rangle_{L^2}$. With $F=D_aX$ and $z=Jv$, this is $\int(Kz_t\cdot z_t+\Omega z_t\cdot z)$ from §4.2. No zero-time-mean condition or positive lower bound is included in the definition. Such conditions enter the coercivity theorem, where $Jv$ becomes a displacement vanishing at both endpoints. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointL2Energy_coercive: On $0<T\le1$, suppose $F_t=MF$, $M_t$ is continuous, $GF=I$, $\|G\|\le D\ge1$, $\|M\|\le L$ with $L\ge0$, and $\langle-(M_t+M^2)w,w\rangle\le|w|^2$. For every $v\in L^2$ with $\int_0^Tv=0$, put $z=Jv$, $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. Then $\int(Kv\cdot v+\Omega v\cdot z)\ge[2D^2(1+L)^2]^{-1}\|v\|_{L^2}^2$. This supplies the positive constant used in Theorem 4.2. The formal statement works in any complete real Hilbert space, with operator fields not necessarily arising from a flow. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_coercive: Let $0\le T\le1$, let $F_t=MF$, $M_t$ be continuous, and let $z_t=v$ with continuous $v$ and $z(0)=z(T)=0$. Assume $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ as a quadratic form. Put $\xi=Fz$, $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. The formal statement proves $\int_0^T(Kv\cdot v+\Omega v\cdot z)\,dt\ge\frac12\int_0^T|M\xi+Fv|^2\,dt$. Here $M\xi+Fv=\xi_t$. It is a result for one label, valid also in a real Hilbert space. The displayed inequality (1.9) includes a further integration over labels, and the weak-path version requires its own extension from continuously differentiable paths.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_eq: For operators $F,M,N$ and vectors $z,v$ in a real Hilbert space, set $\xi=Fz$, $\eta=M\xi+Fv$, $H=-(N+M^2)$, $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. Then $Kv\cdot v+\Omega v\cdot z=|\eta|^2-H\xi\cdot\xi-(\eta\cdot M\xi+\xi\cdot N\xi+\xi\cdot M\eta)$. When $F_t=MF$, $z_t=v$, and $N=M_t$, the parenthesized expression is $\partial_t(\xi\cdot M\xi)$. This is the algebra behind (4.7); differentiability and vanishing endpoint values are not hypotheses of this algebraic identity.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointMixedPathCoefficient: At each spatial label, let $K$ and $\Omega$ be bounded operators on $L^2([0,T];\mathbb R^3)$, varying half-Hölder continuously with the label, and take $T\ge0$. Define $B=K-J\Omega$, where $J$ integrates a time path from zero. Thus $J$ acts after $\Omega$. When these operators are multiplication by the time-dependent matrices, this is $Bv=Kv-J(\Omega v)$ in Appendix A. The formula does not impose zero time mean, divergence freedom or coercivity; those are separate ingredients in the projected equation $\mathcal RBv=-\mathcal RL$.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointMixedPathCoefficient_: On $[0,1]$, let $v\in L^2$ have zero integral. At a fixed label $a$, suppose applying the supplied bounded path operators to this particular $v$ agrees almost everywhere with $K(t,a)v(t)$ and $\Omega(t,a)v(t)$, respectively. Then $\langle(K-J\Omega)v,v\rangle_{L^2}=\int_0^1(Kv\cdot v+\Omega v\cdot Jv)\,dt$, where $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$. The left side uses the supplied operators and the right side uses the coefficient matrices. Agreement on every other path is not required. This is the energy identity preceding Appendix A.1. The lower bound $\mu\|v\|_{L^2}^2$ is a separate displacement-energy assumption, not a conclusion of this identity.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointPhysicalForcePrimitiv: For a matrix field $F(t,a)$ and a force $f_{\mathrm{lab}}(t,a)$ already written in labels, define $L(t,a)=-\int_0^tF(s,a)^Tf_{\mathrm{lab}}(s,a)\,ds$. The torus label is represented by its periodic lift to $\mathbb R^3$. In Theorem 4.2, $F=D_aX$ and $f_{\mathrm{lab}}=f\circ X$, giving the paper's source and $L(0)=0$. This expression neither performs the composition with $X$ nor imposes regularity. To treat it as a differentiable force primitive, one supplies the integrability and smoothness hypotheses used by the subsequent existence theorem.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive: For a function $v:\mathbb R\to E$ into a real normed space, define $Jv(t)=\int_0^tv(s)\,ds$ using the oriented vector-valued integral. Thus negative $t$ reverses the integration direction, and $Jv(0)=0$. The integral expression is assigned zero when the integrand is not integrable; the integral in a noncomplete target is also assigned zero. These defaults do not assert differentiability or recover a displacement. On a positive finite interval, an $L^2$ velocity with values in a complete real normed space has an absolutely continuous primitive with derivative $v$ almost everywhere, and zero time mean gives $Jv(T)=0$. The endpoint construction uses continuous curves in complete function spaces, so its integrals have their ordinary meaning. The definition itself imposes none of that regularity.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointPrimitiveLp_inner_eq_: Let $T\ge0$ and let $u,v\in L^2([0,T];E)$ for a complete real Hilbert space. If $\int_0^Tv=0$, then $\langle Ju,v\rangle_{L^2}=-\langle u,Jv\rangle_{L^2}$. Only the second path needs zero mean. This is the pairing identity used in Appendix A to turn $\langle(K-J\Omega)v,v\rangle$ into the displacement energy. The conclusion is an identity of integrals, not the paper's pointwise formula for $J^*v$; its application to the energy requires no pointwise choice of an $L^2$ representative. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive_eq_neg_term: Assume $v$ is integrable on $[0,T]$ and $\int_0^Tv(s)\,ds=0$. For every $t\in[0,T]$, its primitive satisfies $Jv(t)=-\int_t^Tv(s)\,ds$. The conclusion identifies the displacement obtained from the initial endpoint with the same displacement recovered from the terminal endpoint. This is the equality used before Cauchy–Schwarz in §4.1. Continuity and differentiability of $v$ are unnecessary; in particular the statement applies to the square-integrable velocities representing $H^1_0$ displacements. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointPrimitive_terminal_po: For $T\ge0$, let $v\in L^2([0,T];E)$ have zero time integral and put $z(t)=\int_0^tv(s)\,ds$. Then $\int_0^T\|z(t)\|^2\,dt\le(T^2/2)\int_0^T\|v(t)\|^2\,dt$. The formal statement allows a general real normed target space and does not require $T\le1$. For $E=\mathbb R^3$ it is exactly the second inequality in (4.5), with $z\in H^1_0$. The factor $1/2$ comes from integrating the terminal Cauchy–Schwarz estimate, rather than from a sharp Poincaré constant.

Let $v\in L^2([0,T];E)$ have zero integral, and let $t\in[0,T]$. For $z(t)=\int_0^tv(s)\,ds$, the formal statement gives $\|z(t)\|^2\le(T-t)\int_0^T\|v(s)\|^2\,ds$. It follows from the terminal representation $z(t)=-\int_t^Tv$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. This is the first bound in (4.5), with exactly the factor $T-t$. Neither a restriction $T\le1$ nor a three-dimensional target is needed; the paper's Sobolev displacement is a special case.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointProjectedHilbertOpera: Let $V$ be a closed subspace of a real Hilbert space and $K$ a bounded operator. If $\langle Kv,v\rangle\ge\kappa\|v\|^2$ for every $v\in V$, with $\kappa>0$, then $v\mapsto P_VKv$ is injective on $V$, where $P_V$ is the orthogonal projection. In Appendix A.2, $V$ is the space of divergence-free spatial $L^2$ fields. This identifies two velocities solving the same fixed-time equation. The formal statement gives injectivity only; it does not assert surjectivity or a Hölder estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointProjectedWeak_eq_mean: If $w\in L^2([0,T];E)$ satisfies $w-T^{-1}\int_0^Tw=0$ in that space, then $w(t)=T^{-1}\int_0^Tw$ for almost every time. Appendix A.2 uses $T=1$ to recover the constant removed by $\mathcal Q$. This result alone supplies neither spatial Leray projection nor spatial Hölder regularity. The formal statement is meaningful even for zero interval length because the reciprocal at zero is assigned zero and the almost-everywhere assertion is then vacuous; the endpoint argument uses $T>0$.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointRecoveredPrimitive_ha: Let $T\ge0$, and let an injective bounded linear map embed a Banach space $X$ into another Banach space $Y$. Suppose $v:[0,T]\to X$ is continuous, its image agrees almost everywhere with a $Y$-valued path $w$, and $\int_0^Tw=0$. Then $Jv(0)=Jv(T)=0$ and $(Jv)_t=v$ throughout the interval, with derivatives taken from within it. In Appendix A.2, the embedding passes from the strong spatial norm to the weak one. Injectivity makes the recovered zero mean valid in the stronger space as well. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointSpatialWeakErrorEstim: Let $\mathcal R$ be a bounded linear map on half-Hölder fields on the unit torus with values in a real Hilbert space. Assume $\langle\mathcal Rw,v\rangle_{L^2}=\langle w,v\rangle_{L^2}$ for every $w$ and every fixed field $v=\mathcal Rv$. Let $B\in C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;\mathcal L(H))$ and suppose $\langle B(a)v(a),v(a)\rangle\ge\mu\|v(a)\|^2$ for all such $v$ and all labels, with $\mu>0$. Then $u=\mathcal Ru$ implies $\|u\|_{L^2}\le\min(1,\mu)^{-1}\|\mathcal R(Bu)\|_{L^2}$. Spatial measure has total mass one. The abstract statement does not require idempotence of $\mathcal R$; the paper applies it to a projection. Its bound agrees with the paper's $\mu^{-1}$ bound for $\mu\le1$ and is weaker for $\mu>1$.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointStrongMixedLeray_allS:
On $\mathbb T^3$ with values in $L^2([0,T];\mathbb R^3)$, $T>0$, let $\mathcal R=\mathbb P\mathcal Q$. Suppose $v=\mathcal Rv$, $\mathcal R(Bv)=f$, the base half-Hölder inverse exists, and $B$ is pointwise coercive on the projected fields with constant $\mu>0$. Supply actual half-Hölder directional derivatives of $B$ and $f$ through integer order $N$. Then all corresponding derivatives of $v$ exist, remain projected, and satisfy $\mathcal R(BD^
u v)=D^
u f-\mathcal R[D^
u,B]v$. Each norm is bounded by the inverse norm times its source and Leibniz terms involving lower solution derivatives. The statement does not independently construct the base inverse.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointStrongSpatialLeray_al:
Let $v$ be a solenoidal half-Hölder vector field on $\mathbb T^3$ satisfying $\mathbb P(Bv)=f$. Assume this projected coefficient map already has a bounded inverse and $B$ is pointwise coercive on projected fields with a positive constant. Supply genuine half-Hölder directional derivatives of $B$ and $f$ through order $N$. Then the corresponding derivatives of $v$ exist, stay divergence free, and satisfy $\mathbb P(BD^
u v)=D^
u f-\mathbb P[D^
u,B]v$, with norm bounds using the inverse norm and lower derivatives. This supplies the differentiated equations in Lemma A.2, rather than proving the initial inverse theorem.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointSubtractMean: For an $L^2$ path on $[0,T]$, the operator is $\mathcal Qv=v-T^{-1}\int_0^Tv(s)\,ds$, where the average is viewed as a constant path. When $T=1$ this is the projection used in Appendix A. For $T>0$ its range consists of zero-time-mean paths, whose primitives have both zero endpoint values. The formula is defined even at $T=0$ by assigning zero to the reciprocal there; that case is not an averaging operation on a positive interval. The definition alone does not assert orthogonality or compatibility with spatial projection.
notes.TorusEuler.endpointWeakInstant_of_subtra: Let $w\in L^2((0,T];Y)$, let $P:E\to Y$ and $K(t):E\to E$ be bounded linear maps, and let $v,h,L$ be $E$-valued functions. Suppose $w=P(Kv-h+L)$ almost everywhere and $w-T^{-1}\int_0^Tw=0$ in $L^2$. Then $P(Kv)=c+Ph-PL$ almost everywhere, where $c=T^{-1}\int_0^Tw$. The function $h$ is arbitrary in this statement. Substituting $h=J(\Omega v)$, $P=\mathbb P$ and $T=1$ gives (A.9). No continuity or invertibility is asserted. The formula is also defined for $T\le0$: the restricted time measure is zero, so the almost-everywhere conclusion is vacuous; at $T=0$ the reciprocal is assigned zero.
notes.TorusEuler.eulerianMomentum_of_strongLab: At a specified time, suppose $F_t=MF$, $v_t$ exists, and $F$ has a bounded right inverse. If $F^TFv_t+F^Tq_x=F^Tf-2F^TMFv$, then $B=Fv$ has a time derivative and satisfies $B_t+MB+q_x=f$. Here $q_x$ denotes the pressure gradient expressed in physical coordinates along the trajectory. The conclusion is pointwise in a real Hilbert space. In Theorem 4.2 it is the momentum conversion after setting $F=D_aX$; the spatial change of variables and incompressibility still require separate flow identities.
notes.TorusEuler.even_fderiv_of_odd: For an odd map $f:E\to F$ between real normed spaces, the formal statement says that its derivative expression is even: $Df(-x)=Df(x)$. No differentiability assumption is present. At a point where a derivative does not exist, the formalization assigns the derivative expression the zero linear map; symmetry preserves the set of differentiability points. For the smooth velocity and flow in §5.1 this is the ordinary differentiation of $f(-x)=-f(x)$. It explains evenness of their derivative matrices. Applying it to $U$ alone does not prove that the flow is odd; that uses uniqueness of trajectories separately.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_endpointContinuousRepr: Let $X,E,Y$ be real normed spaces, $j:X\to Y$ and $P:E\to X$ bounded linear maps, and $S(t):X\to X$ bounded isomorphisms. On $[0,T]$, assume $S(t)^{-1}$ is operator-norm continuous with norm at most $M\ge0$, and $h,L$ are continuous with bounds $C_h,C_L$. Let $S_w(t)$ be injective operators on $Y$ with $S_w(t)j=jS(t)$. If $S_w(t)w(t)=j(c+Ph(t)-PL(t))$ almost everywhere, then $v(t)=S(t)^{-1}(c+Ph(t)-PL(t))$ is continuous, satisfies the strong equation at every time, and $jv=w$ almost everywhere. Its norm is at most $M(\|c\|+\|P\|(C_h+C_L))$. Injectivity of $j$ and completeness of these spaces are not hypotheses here. Appendix A.2 uses an actual inclusion into spatial $L^2$, with $h=J(\Omega w)$. The final polynomial bound requires the preceding estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_endpointSpatialLerayIn: On $\mathbb T^3$, suppose $K$ is a matrix-valued half-Hölder field with Lipschitz bound $L\ge0$, and $\langle K(a)w,w\rangle\ge\mu|w|^2$ for every $a,w$, with $\mu>0$. Then $v\mapsto\mathbb P(Kv)$ is a bounded isomorphism on divergence-free $C^{0,1/2}$ fields. An absolute $C\ge0$, chosen before $K,\mu,L$, gives inverse norm at most $C(4+\mu^{-1}+\|K\|_\infty+L)^{145}$. Symmetry of $K$ is not assumed. This is the spatial base inverse underlying Lemma A.2; the paper only needs some fixed polynomial power and assumes stronger coefficient regularity.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_forward_flowJetBounds: Fix a nonnegative sequence $R_n$. For $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, and a smooth unit-periodic velocity with flow $X$, assume $\|DX\|,\|DX^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D$ and $\|D^kU\|_\infty\le R_n\mathsf D^k$ for every $2\le k\le n$. There are $C_n\ge0$, chosen before the parent, such that $\|D_a^nX\|_\infty\le C_n\mathsf D^{5n-4}$ for every $n\ge1$. These are multilinear operator norms, equivalent to the paper’s coordinate sums up to order-dependent constants. Exponent subtraction is among nonnegative integers; the asserted range $n\ge1$ makes $5n-4$ the ordinary integer value.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_freezing_split_sources: Let $B$ be a bounded half-Hölder operator-valued coefficient on a metric label space, with Lipschitz constant $L\ge0$, and let $v\in C^{0,1/2}$. For $0<r\le1$ and a center $a_0$, the error $(B(a_0)-B(a))v(a)$ splits into two half-Hölder fields. The near field has norm at most $8L\sqrt r\,\|v\|_{C^{0,1/2}}$; the far field vanishes for $d(a,a_0)\le r$ and has supremum norm at most $2\|B\|_\infty\|v\|_\infty$. These are the sources in (A.7). No inverse operator is applied by this statement.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_halfHolderWords_norm_l: Let a periodic field on $\mathbb R^3$ represent an element of $C^{n,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;E)$, for an integer $n\ge0$. Then its successive ordered coordinate derivatives through order $n$ can all be represented as half-Hölder fields on the torus, with their differentiation identities satisfied. Each has norm at most $\sqrt2\|f\|_{C^{n,1/2}}$. The base norm is the maximum of supremum and half-Hölder seminorm; the higher norm sums these quantities for Fréchet derivatives. This supplies actual derivatives for Lemma A.2, not an estimate for a solution whose higher regularity is still unknown.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_iteratedDeriv_waveProf: For every integer $j\ge2$, the formal statement chooses a positive constant $C_j$ such that $|\partial_s^jF_h(s)|\le C_jh^{1-j}$ for all $0<h\le1$ and all real phases $s$. The family $F_h$ is the particular normalized bump construction. The order $j$ is chosen before the constant, and the constant is chosen before $h$ and $s$; no uniform bound in $j$ is asserted. The power uses the integer exponent $1-j$, rather than subtraction of nonnegative integers, so it means $h^{-(j-1)}$. This is the derivative scaling stated in Lemma 3.1.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_jointSmooth_oscillator: Assume $0<T$, $\kappa(0,a)\ne0$, $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$, periodic smooth coefficients, and $f(t,a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)=f(t,a,s)$ with phase period one. Smooth coefficients and a smooth source with zero phase mean produce a jointly smooth solution of (5.15), with zero initial velocity and normalized pressure. Periodicity and the compatibility of label and phase translations are retained. When the coefficients and source have the required reflection symmetry or support, the solution inherits it. This existence result leaves uniqueness to a separate argument.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_norm_iteratedFDeriv_pe: Let $K,S\subset\mathbb R^3$ be compact and suppose $x-y\notin\mathbb Z^3$ for every $x\in K,y\in S$. There is an open $U\supset K$ such that, for each integer $d\ge0$, a constant $C\ge0$ bounds the difference of the $d$th spatial derivatives of two far pressure gradients on $U$ by $C\int_{S\cap Q}|P-Q_1|$. Here $Q$ is a unit cell and $P,Q_1$ are integrable complex matrix fields; the pressure is the real-valued integral against the periodic pressure kernel. The constant is chosen before these fields and the observation point. This proves smoothing across separation on the torus. Identifying this pressure gradient with the localized Leray-divergence term in Proposition 8.4 requires the adjoining representation theorem.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryPhaseSolve_: On $[l,r]$, $l\le r$, assume continuous $M$, a transported covector satisfying $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ and $\kappa(l)\ne0$. Let $f(t,s)$ be period one with zero phase mean and continuous in time in the supremum norm on bounded continuous phase functions. The formal statement constructs a continuous period-one velocity $V$ with $V(l)=0$, $\kappa\cdot V=0$ and $\langle V\rangle_s=0$. Its normalized periodic pressure satisfies $V_t+MV+\kappa\partial_s\pi=f$, with $\langle\pi\rangle_s=0$. Derivatives are asserted pointwise in phase and within the time interval. This solves (1.12) at one particle label after inserting its forcing; regularity in the label and the specific hierarchy source are additional ingredients.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryTransverse_: Let $t_0\in[l,r]$, with continuous coefficients $M,f$, and suppose $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ with $\kappa(t_0)\ne0$. For any initial amplitude $V_0\perp\kappa(t_0)$, the formal statement constructs $V$ on $[l,r]$ with $V(t_0)=V_0$, $\kappa\ne0$ and $\kappa\cdot V=0$. It satisfies $V_t+MV+p_s\kappa=f$, where $|\kappa|^2p_s=\kappa\cdot f-2\kappa\cdot MV$. The conclusion extends to times before $t_0$ as well as after it. Setting $f=0$ recovers the seed equation (3.2) along a single label. No smooth dependence on labels or periodic phase pressure is asserted by this one-path theorem.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_paperA1_smoothSolution: On $[0,1]\times\mathbb T^3$, let $K,\Omega,L$ be jointly smooth. Require $K,\Omega$ to be time-continuous in $C^{0,1/2}$, with uniform bounds on values and first spatial derivatives. Assume $K\ge\kappa I$ as quadratic forms, $\kappa>0$, and $\int_0^1(Kz_t\cdot z_t+\Omega z_t\cdot z)\,dt\ge\mu\int_0^1|z_t|^2\,dt$ at every label for every $z\in H^1_0$, with $\mu>0$. Then there exist a continuous divergence-free half-Hölder velocity $v$ and a time-independent divergence-free field $c$ such that $Jv(1)=0$ and $\mathbb P(Kv-J(\Omega v)+L)=c$. The periodic lift of $v$ is jointly smooth. Here $Jw(t)=\int_0^tw(s)\,ds$. Symmetry of $K$ and skew-symmetry of $\Omega$ are not hypotheses. This intermediate result constructs the smooth velocity; the full theorem supplies the other recovered smooth fields.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_paperPhysicalStepBudge: Fix nonnegative integer exponents for the envelope, hierarchy loss and mean estimates, a finite depth $P$, and nonnegative constants for the coefficient, remainder, leading-wave, pressure and flow bounds. There exists $\Gamma_P$ such that the common expression $\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b$ dominates every listed cost simultaneously for all $\mathsf D\ge1$, with $b=6r+5a+2a_{\rm mean}+160$. In particular $\Gamma_P\ge1$. This is a finite numerical choice of constants before the parent scale, as required for $C_{\rm step}$ in §5.6. Its coefficient may depend on the supplied estimates and depth. The result does not prove those estimates or assert the smallness condition involving $\lambda$.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_paper_hierarchy_invers: Assume $0\le t_0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$, $\lambda=|\kappa(t_0,0)|\ge1$, smooth periodic $U$, gradient and both deformation bounds $\mathsf D$, velocity derivative bounds $R_n\mathsf D^j$, and central transverse stability and coupling bounds $\mathsf D,\mathsf D^{-1}$. Put $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$, $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$ and choose a sufficiently small radius. Smooth transverse solutions on $[t_0,T]$ satisfy $\|V\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_n\mathsf D^{20}(\gamma(t_0)^{-1}\|V(t_0)\|_{[n]}+\|f\|_{[n],\gamma})$. Initial data and source are supported within $2\ell_*$ of lattice points and satisfy phase period one and the coupled label translations. Unlike the numbered lemma’s first clause, this theorem assumes no smooth extension before activation. The transverse stability assumption is $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$ for every transverse homogeneous solution $\mathbf b$ and $t_0\le t'\le t\le T$.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_parentDerivedLowBounds:
There is an absolute lower frequency threshold such that the following holds on $[0,T]$, $T>0$. Let $u$ be a smooth periodic velocity, $\|u(t)\|_\infty\le\mu$, with Fourier support at most $2\mu^5$, and let a continuous periodic residual satisfy $\|R(t)\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-3}$, where $\lambda\ge1$. Assume $u_t=-\mathbb P((u\cdot
abla)u)+R$, with the advective term represented in the spatial one-half Hölder space. For $\mu$ above the threshold, the formal statement gives $\|
abla u(t,x)\|\le\mu^9$ and $\|\partial_t
abla u(t,x)\|\le\mu^{18}$ for every point and time in the closed interval. Time derivatives at the endpoints are taken from within the interval; matrix norms are operator norms. This supplies (7.6) without requiring oddness.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_parentMeanWeightedCoef: Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, and let $X$ be the flow of a smooth unit-periodic $U$. Assume $\|D_aX\|,\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D$ and $\|D^jU\|_\infty\le R_n\mathsf D^j$ for every $1\le j\le n$, where the nonnegative sequence $R_n$ is fixed before the flow. Write $F=D_aX$, $G=F^{-1}$, $M=(DU)\circ X$, $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. Let $\ell_*>0$ and $\ell_*\mathsf D^6\le1$. All spatial half-Hölder derivative sets of $F,F^T,K,\Omega$ are bounded. Nonnegative sequences $C_n,H_m$, chosen before the flow, satisfy $\|F\|_{[n],1/2},\|F^T\|_{[n],1/2}\le C_n\mathsf D/\sqrt{\ell_*}$. For every individual word $\alpha$ of $m\ge1$ coordinate derivatives, $\ell_*^m(\|\partial^\alpha K\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}}+\|\partial^\alpha\Omega\|_{C_tC^{0,1/2}})\le H_m\mathsf D^9\sqrt{\ell_*}$. Summing the finitely many words changes only the order-dependent constant.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_parentResidualWeighted: Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, $\lambda\ge1$, $\ell_*\ge0$, $\ell_*\mathsf D^6\le1$, and let $X$ be the flow of a smooth unit-periodic $U$, with $\|DX\|,\|DX^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D$. Fix nonnegative $V_n$ and assume $\|D^kU\|_\infty\le V_n\mathsf D^k$ for all $n\ge2$ and $2\le k\le n$. For any family of continuous torus fields $R(t)$ with Fourier radius $4\mathsf D$ and $\|R(t)\|_\infty\le\lambda^{-5/2}$, every scaled label norm of $R\circ X$ is finite and $\|R\circ X\|_{[n]}\le C_n\lambda^{-5/2}$, uniformly on $[0,T]$. The constants $C_n$ depend only on the sequence $V_n$ and are chosen before $U$, $X$ and the fields. This need not be the momentum residual of $U$; that identification is supplied in the application.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_parentVelocityJetBound: There is a nonnegative sequence $V_n$, chosen before the field and $\mathsf D$, with the following property. Let $g$ be continuous on the unit torus, have Fourier support $|k|\le4\mathsf D$, and satisfy $\|Dg\|_\infty\le\mathsf D$ with $\mathsf D\ge1$. Then $\|D^kg\|_\infty\le V_n\mathsf D^k$ for every $1\le k\le n$. Derivatives refer to the periodic lift and use multilinear operator norms. Finite Fourier support supplies spatial smoothness; no time dependence or Euler equation is required. The result gives no bound for the undifferentiated field.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_parent_coefficientJetB: Let $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge1$, and let $X$ be the flow of a smooth unit-periodic $U$. Assume $\|D_aX\|,\|(D_aX)^{-1}\|\le\mathsf D$ and $\|D^jU\|_\infty\le R_n\mathsf D^j$ for every $1\le j\le n$, where the nonnegative sequence $R_n$ is fixed before the flow. Put $F=DX$, $G=F^{-1}$, $M=DU\circ X$ and $\kappa=G^Tk_*$. Suppose $t_0\in[0,T]$ and $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda>0$. There are $C_n\ge0$, fixed before the flow, bounding the order-$n$ derivatives of $F$, $G$ and $G^T$, $M$, $\kappa/\lambda$, $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2$, and $P_\kappa$ by $C_n$ times $\mathsf D^{5n+1}$, $\mathsf D^{7n+1}$, $\mathsf D^{6n+1}$, $\mathsf D^{7n+2}$, $\mathsf D^{16n+4}$, and $\mathsf D^{16n+8}$, respectively. All bounds are uniform in time and label. No residual, pressure or coercivity assumption is used.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_parent_genericLeading_: Fix parent derivative bounds $\|D^jU\|\le W_n\mathsf D^j$ for $1\le j\le n$. Suppose $0<T\le1$, $\mathsf D\ge2$, $\lambda\ge1$, the smooth periodic parent flow and its inverse have derivative norm at most $\mathsf D$, and $|\kappa(t_0,0)|=\lambda$, $|k_*|\le\mathsf D\lambda$. Let the central seed satisfy (5.5) and $|\mathbf a(t,0)|\le\lambda^{-3/4}$. For sufficiently large integer $a$ and $\ell_*^{-1}=\mathsf D^a$, every localized seed smooth jointly in $(t,a)$ on $[t_0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$ and every admissible cutoff yield $D_x^2\mathsf p_1^\natural\le C\mathsf D^{2a+74}\lambda^{-1/4}I$ on $[0,T]$. The periodic continuation is constructed from this local regularity. Constants precede the parent. The conclusion is an upper quadratic-form bound for the leading pressure only; it does not bound its absolute Hessian norm or the complete pressure correction.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_periodic_offOrigin_cut: Let $K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$ be compact, representing observation points away from the torus origin. The formal statement produces a smooth period-one function $0\le\chi\le1$, an open neighbourhood of $K$ on which $\chi=1$, and an open neighbourhood of the entire integer lattice on which $\chi=0$. The closed support of $\chi$ avoids the lattice. Moreover, for $x\in K$ and $y$ in the closed support of $1-\chi$, the difference $x-y$ is never an integer lattice vector. Thus the source and observation points are separated on the torus, not merely in one chosen cube. This is the cutoff used for the local and far pressure split in Proposition 8.4.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_spatialHolderHalfNorm_: Fix an integer $n\ge0$. Suppose a periodic field and all its ordered coordinate derivatives through order $n$ are represented by half-Hölder fields, with the actual differentiation identities, and every such field has norm at most $K\ge0$. Then the $C^{n,1/2}$ norm of the original field is at most $C_nK$, where $C_n$ is chosen before the fields and $K$. This converts the differentiated-equation estimates in Lemma A.2 into the paper's full higher norm. Arbitrary bounded fields with derivative labels would not satisfy the required differentiation hypotheses.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_terminalSmoothExtensio: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $F$ a real Banach space, $O\subset E$ open, and $a<T$. If $f:[a,T]\times O\to F$ is jointly smooth up to the time boundary, the formal statement gives $g$ smooth on $(a,\infty)\times O$ and equal to $f$ on the entire original closed slab. Values of $g$ are defined elsewhere but have no asserted regularity there. This is the extension step needed in the auxiliary note. Seeley's theorem on page 625 supplies a continuous linear extension operator; this formal conclusion asserts existence for each field and does not state linearity or continuity of a choice of extension. It imposes no differential equation beyond $T$.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_truncatedParentPoisson:

A jointly smooth periodic pressure $p$ exists with zero integral over the centered unit cell and $\Delta p=-\operatorname{tr}((
abla u)^2)$. Moreover $u_t+u\cdot

abla u)$ on the closed interval, with time derivatives taken from within it. This supplies the pressure choice and projected residual formula in §5.1. The theorem does not require $u$ to solve Euler and does not conclude that this residual vanishes.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_uniform_freezingHalfHo: Let $r(\xi)$ be orthogonal projections on a real Hilbert space with a compatible complete complexification, smooth for $\xi\ne0$, with $\|D^ir(\xi)\|\le D^i$ for $0\le i\le5$ on $1/2\le|\xi|\le2$, where $D\ge1$. Suppose $B$ has coercivity $\mu>0$ on every projected range, including the zero-frequency range. Put $Q=2+\mu^{-1}+\|B\|$. The formal statement bounds the two Fourier operators constructed from the inverse symbols by $CQ^{11}$ on $C^{0,1/2}$. For $r_0>0$ and a source vanishing in the closed $r_0$-ball about $a$, the second operator has increments at most $KQ^{11}r_0^{-1}\|f\|_\infty d(a,b)$ when $d(a,b)\le r_0/4$. The constants depend only on $D$ and the fixed cutoff. Identifying these operators with $A_0(D)^{-1}$ and $A_0(D)^{-1}\mathcal R$ uses the separate Fourier identity, which also assumes degree-zero homogeneity. This estimate alone does not impose homogeneity; the paper's Leray symbols have it.
notes.TorusEuler.exists_waveSwitch_scheduled_w: There is a fixed constant $C\ge0$ depending only on the chosen smooth time transition. Let $r>0$, $\lambda_+>0$, and suppose $|\gamma(t)|\le e^{3-4\log\lambda_+}$ on $[t_0,t_0+1/r]$. If $Cre^3\le\mu$, the formal theorem gives $|\widetilde\chi'(t)|\,|\gamma(t)|\le\mu\lambda_+^{-4}$ for every real $t$, where $\widetilde\chi(t)=1-\chi(1+r(t-t_0))$. The weight need not be continuous or bounded outside the switching interval, because the cutoff derivative vanishes there. With $\lambda_+=\lambda_{j+1}$ this is the numerical implication used in (7.10), conditional on the early-gain and rate bounds.
notes.TorusEuler.fderiv_frozenSymbol_inverse_a: Let $r$ be an orthogonal projection on a real Hilbert space, and suppose $\langle Bw,w\rangle\ge\mu\|w\|^2$ on its range, with $\mu>0$. Set $A=rBr+I-r$. The derivative of the inverse as $r$ varies in direction $h$ is $D(A^{-1})[h]=-A^{-1}(hBr+rBh-h)A^{-1}$. Coercivity ensures that $A$ is invertible at the point of differentiation. The formal statement concerns variations of the real operator $r$; composing with the frequency-dependent projection and passing to complex Fourier coefficients are additional steps needed in Appendix A.1.
notes.TorusEuler.fderiv_lift_realVectorFourier: Let $g$ and $d$ be continuous $\mathbb R^3$-valued fields on $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3$. Suppose the periodic lift of $g$ is continuously differentiable and the lift of $d$ equals $\partial_i g$. The formal statement proves $\partial_i(S_\Lambda g)=S_\Lambda d$ on $\mathbb R^3$. The real cutoff is obtained by applying the finite complex Fourier sum and taking its real part. The identity holds for arbitrary real symbols and scales because the sum is finite; the paper's multiplier interpretation uses its usual smooth symbol and $\Lambda>0$. This is one spatial coordinate derivative, not the complete spatial-and-time commutation clause of Lemma B.1.
notes.TorusEuler.finiteCoefficientPower_iff_mu: For $\mathsf D\ge1$, a nonnegative integer $q$, and a coefficient $c:I\times\mathbb R^3\to A$ in a real normed algebra, the formal statement equates two forms of polynomial control. One bounds the operator norm of every full spatial derivative tensor by $C_m\mathsf D^{q(m+1)}$; the other bounds the sum of coordinate multi-index suprema of order $m$ by the same power, with possibly different constants. Both require smoothness and uniform boundedness in time and space. The conversion changes order-dependent constants but preserves $q$. It does not assert either bound for an arbitrary coefficient, or uniform constants across varying $\mathsf D$ and $c$.
notes.TorusEuler.firstCoupling_cumulative_log_:
Let $
u_i>0$ and $\varepsilon_i\ge0$ for every nonnegative integer $i$. Assume $\varepsilon_{i+1}\le\varepsilon_i/32$ and $|\log(
u_{i+1}/
u_i)|\le2\varepsilon_i$. Then $|\log(
u_n/
u_0)|\le4\varepsilon_0$ for every $n$. All logarithms have positive arguments. In the application, index zero denotes wave one, $
u_0=2\pi$, and $
u_n$ is the first coupling at a later activation. The result requires only these scalar inequalities, not the wave equations. It supplies the accumulated bound by $4\varepsilon_1$ in the paper's indexing; the further estimate by $4(\log N)^{-2}$ requires the gain schedule.
notes.TorusEuler.firstCoupling_pi_bounds:
Let $
u_0=2\pi$, $
u_i>0$ and $\varepsilon_i\ge0$. Suppose $\varepsilon_{i+1}\le\varepsilon_i/32$, $|\log(
u_{i+1}/
u_i)|\le2\varepsilon_i$ for every $i$, and $4\varepsilon_0\le\log2$. The formal statement proves $\pi\le
u_n\le4\pi$ for every $n$. The logarithmic estimate is relative to the positive initial coupling, so exponentiation gives factors between one half and two. In §7.2, these sequences are the couplings at consecutive crossings and their prescribed ratios; index zero here corresponds to wave one. The smallness requirement is explicit, whereas the paper obtains it by taking $N$ sufficiently large.
notes.TorusEuler.firstWaveOrigin_exists: For any real shear parameter $\rho$, final time $T\ge0$ and frequency $\lambda>0$, there are paths $\kappa,\mathbf a:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\kappa(0)=\lambda e_1$ and $\mathbf a(0)=c e_2$, $c>0$. On $[0,T]$ they solve the wave equations over $B_\rho=2\pi(e_1+\rho e_3)\otimes e_2$, remain nonzero and perpendicular, and attain $\max|\mathbf a|=\lambda^{-3/4}$. Only the equations and bounds on this interval are asserted, despite the paths being defined for every real time. No smallness condition on $T\|B_\rho\|$ is required for existence. This is the central wave; it does not yet construct its spatial localization or a new Euler velocity. At $T=0$, derivatives within the singleton interval impose no evolution equation beyond the stipulated values.
notes.TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold: For a finite real cost table $c_k(m,p)$ and nonnegative integers $b,s$, put $K(s)=320b(s+1)$. The formal choice is $\mathcal B(s)=\max\{e^{4K(s+1)^3},\sum_k\sum_{m,p\le7K(s)}|c_k(m,p)|\}$. Thus the finite sum includes order and depth zero, and the exponential term keeps the threshold strictly positive. This is a particular candidate for the threshold requested in §1.5. Its monotonicity, logarithmic lower bound and domination of individual entries are established by separate theorems. The formula does not specify which analytic estimates populate the cost table, and it does not require the original costs to be monotone.
notes.TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold_log_floor: Let $K(s)=320b(s+1)$ and let $\mathcal B(s)$ be the maximum of $e^{4K(s+1)^3}$ and the finite sum of absolute costs through order and depth $7K(s)$. For every nonnegative integer $s$, the formal theorem proves $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$. The positive exponential lower bound justifies taking the ordinary real logarithm. No sign or monotonicity assumption on the cost table is needed, and $b$ may be zero. The paper uses the conclusion only for $b\ge1$ and $s\ge1$. This verifies (1.13) for the explicit threshold, not for an arbitrary function.
notes.TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold_mono: Fix a finite real cost table and a nonnegative integer $b$. With $K(s)=320b(s+1)$, define $\mathcal B(s)$ as the maximum of $e^{4K(s+1)^3}$ and the sum of absolute costs for $m,p\le7K(s)$. The formal theorem proves $\mathcal B(s)\le\mathcal B(t)$ whenever $s\le t$. Increasing the index enlarges the summation ranges and does not decrease the exponential floor; individual costs need not increase with order. The conclusion holds at zero as well as positive indices. This supplies the monotonicity required by §1.5 for this particular threshold and makes no assertion about arbitrary admissible candidates.
notes.TorusEuler.fixedTransverseGenerator: For linear maps $J:S\to E$, $R:E\to S$ and $M:E\to E$, the formal object is the operator $-2RMJ$ on $S$. In §5.4, take $S=k_*^\perp$, $J=A_\perp$ and $R=A_\perp^\dagger$. Then it is the generator of $v_t=-\mathcal M_\perp v+\psi$, where $\mathcal M_\perp=2A_\perp^\dagger MA_\perp$ and $\psi=A_\perp^\dagger f$. This definition alone imposes no flow, invertibility or evolution equation; those hypotheses give it the interpretation in (5.18).
notes.TorusEuler.flowJet_partitionPower_le: Assume $\mathsf D\ge1$ and a partition of $n$ into $k\ge2$ strictly positive parts. Every exponent $5n_i-4$ is therefore nonnegative despite subtraction being truncated at zero. In the recurrence (5.9), a partition into at least two positive parts produces a power no larger than $\mathsf D^{5n-4}$ after inserting the lower-order estimates. This is the exponent calculation displayed in Proposition 5.1. It closes the induction on $n$; the remaining finite partition sum contributes only to the order-dependent constant.
notes.TorusEuler.freezingCoefficientLine: For a half-Hölder operator-valued field $B$ on the torus, define $B_s=(1-s)I+sB$. This expression is defined for every real $s$. The continuation argument in Lemma A.2 uses only $0\le s\le1$, where coercivity of $B$ gives a common positive lower bound for the path. At $s=0$, multiplication by $B_s$ is the identity; at $s=1$ it is multiplication by $B$. The definition by itself asserts neither coercivity nor invertibility of the projected operators.
notes.TorusEuler.freezingContinuationLine_isUn: Let $S$ be a bounded operator on a Banach space. Suppose a fixed $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|v\|\le M\|((1-s)I+sS)v\|$ for every vector $v$ and every $s\in[0,1]$. Then every operator on this segment is invertible. In particular $S$ is invertible. This is the continuation principle used at the end of Lemma A.2, where successive local inversions are obtained by Neumann series. The uniform estimate is assumed for the entire segment; a lower bound for $S$ alone would not be this hypothesis.
notes.TorusEuler.freezingCutoff: For a center $a_0$ and radius $r$, define $\chi(a)=\max\{0,\min\{1,2-d(a,a_0)/r\}\}$. If $r>0$, this is one on the closed $r$-ball, zero at distances at least $2r$, and linear in the distance between them. It is the cutoff used for the error splitting in (A.7). The formal construction uses its Lipschitz bound, not a differentiable cutoff. At $r=0$, division by zero is assigned zero and this formula gives $\chi=1$ everywhere. The support and localization conclusions are only asserted for positive radius.
notes.TorusEuler.freezingCutoff_eq_one: Let $r>0$, and use $\chi(a)=\max\{0,\min\{1,2-d(a,a_0)/r\}\}$. If $d(a,a_0)\le r$, then $\chi(a)=1$. This includes the boundary of the inner ball. Consequently the far source $(1-\chi)(B(a_0)-B)v$ vanishes there. That is the support fact required in the freezing argument for (A.7). The statement concerns only the values of this cutoff; no smoothness of the cutoff or coefficient and no inverse estimate is required.
notes.TorusEuler.freezingCutoff_eq_zero: Let $r>0$ and $\chi(a)=\max\{0,\min\{1,2-d(a,a_0)/r\}\}$. If $d(a,a_0)\ge2r$, then $\chi(a)=0$. Thus the near source $\chi(B(a_0)-B)v$ vanishes outside the radius-$2r$ neighborhood and also on its boundary. This is the support property used in (A.7), valid on an arbitrary metric space. It gives no derivative estimate and does not require the cutoff to be smooth.
notes.TorusEuler.freezingCutoff_lipschitz: For $r>0$, the cutoff $\chi(a)=\max\{0,\min\{1,2-d(a,a_0)/r\}\}$ satisfies $|\chi(a)-\chi(b)|\le r^{-1}d(a,b)$ on a metric label space. This is the precise regularity used by the formal localization argument. The paper writes $|\nabla\chi|\le C/r$, while this piecewise linear radial cutoff need not be differentiable at the transition radii. The difference bound gives the needed control of $\chi(B(a_0)-B)$ without asserting a classical gradient everywhere.
notes.TorusEuler.freezingCutoff_mem_Icc: On a metric space, for every center $a_0$, every real radius $r$ and every point $a$, the expression $\chi(a)=\max\{0,\min\{1,2-d(a,a_0)/r\}\}$ lies in $[0,1]$. No positivity of $r$ is needed for this range statement. At $r=0$, the formal division convention gives $d(a,a_0)/0=0$, hence $\chi=1$ everywhere. Positive radius is needed for the inner-ball, outer-ball and Lipschitz conclusions used in (A.7). The statement here bounds the two factors $\chi$ and $1-\chi$; it does not by itself provide spatial localization.
notes.TorusEuler.freezingHaarEmbedding_line_co: Let $v$ be a half-Hölder Hilbert-space-valued field on the unit torus and suppose $\langle B(a)v(a),v(a)\rangle\ge\mu\|v(a)\|^2$ at every label. For $0\le s\le1$, $B_s=(1-s)I+sB$ satisfies $\langle B_sv,v\rangle_{L^2_a}\ge\min(1,\mu)\|v\|_{L^2_a}^2$. Spatial measure is normalized to give the unit torus mass one. This is the integrated coercivity used in Lemma A.2. The formal inequality does not require $\mu>0$; positivity is needed when this bound is used to obtain an inverse.
notes.TorusEuler.freezingHalfHolderMultipliers: Let $r(\xi)$ be smooth away from zero, homogeneous of degree zero, and orthogonal, with $B$ coercive on every projected range by $\mu>0$. Suppose half-Hölder fields satisfy, mode by mode, $\widehat v=r\widehat v$, $\widehat f=r\widehat w$ and $\widehat s=B\widehat v-\widehat w$. Then $v=A_0(D)^{-1}f+A_0(D)^{-1}\mathcal Rs$, where $A_0=rBr+I-r$. This is the identity underlying (A.7), with the Fourier identities explicitly supplied. It keeps one coefficient-error source $s$; producing the near and far sources and splitting the last term by linearity are separate steps.
notes.TorusEuler.freezing_torus_absorb_supremu: Let $f,v\in C^{0,1/2}(\mathbb T^3;H)$, with the norm given by the maximum of supremum and half-Hölder seminorm, and use normalized torus measure for $L^2$. Suppose $K\ge1$, $\|v\|\le2(C\|f\|+K\|v\|_\infty)$, and $\|v\|_{L^2}\le\mu^{-1}\|f\|$. Then $\|v\|\le4(C+K(4K)^3\mu^{-1})\|f\|$. The statement assumes the weak estimate exactly as written; neither $C\ge0$ nor $\mu>0$ is a separate hypothesis. At $\mu=0$, its reciprocal is assigned zero and the weak premise forces $v=0$. The application to (A.5) obtains the weak bound from positive coercivity and separately controls $C,K$ by the coefficient parameters.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencyExponent: For nonnegative integers $b,s$, the formal definition is the nonnegative integer $K(s)=320b(s+1)$. The paper uses it with $b\ge1$ and $s\ge1$, giving $K(s)\ge640$. In the recurrence $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{K(q_j)}$, the frequencies are real numbers but the exponent is an integer; no rounding or real-power convention is involved. The same $K(s)$ determines the cutoff $7K(s)$ on derivative orders and expansion depths entering the threshold. The definition also permits $b=0$, in which case $K(s)=0$; the construction’s separate hypothesis $b\ge1$ excludes that case.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_child_veloc: Let $\mu\ge2$, integers $b\ge1$ and $m\le q\le q_+$, and put $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q+1)}$, $\lambda_+=\lambda^{320b(q_++1)}$. Suppose $U_+=V+v$ and $V=U+O+\bar W$. Assume $\bar W,v$ have finite spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ bounds, with $\|\bar W\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le C\mu^{9b(m+2)}\lambda^{-5/2}$, $C\le\mu$, and $\|v\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le\lambda^{5m}\lambda_+^{-5}$. Then $U_+-U-O$ also has the required Hölder regularity and norm at most $\lambda^{-1}$. This statement is for fields at one time; applying it at every time gives the numerical bound in (7.4), but does not by itself assert continuity in time. The spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm is $\sum_{i\le m}(\sup|D^if|+[D^if]_{1/2})$, where $D^if$ is the full $i$th derivative tensor in operator norm.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_commonLifet: Let $\lambda_0\ge4^{16}$ and define $\tau_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{-1/8}(4\log\lambda_{j+2})^3$ for $j\ge1$. Assume $0<\tau_j\le\lambda_{j-1}^{-1/16}$, $4\tau_{j+1}\le\tau_j$, $t_1=t_2=0$, $t_{j+1}-t_j\le\tau_j$, and strict increase from $t_2$ onward. Let $S_0=1$ and $S_j=t_j+2\tau_j$. Then a positive finite $T_\infty$ exists with $t_j\to T_\infty$, every $t_j<T_\infty<S_j$, and $T_\infty-t_j\le4\tau_j/3$. The formal sequences also assign $t_0=0$. Its internal half-length indexed by $i$ is the paper's $\tau_{i+1}$; the displayed conclusion above uses the paper's indexing. No solution of the Euler equations is asserted by this scalar time estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_endpointSla: Define positive half-lengths $\tau_j$ for $j\ge1$ by $\tau_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{-1/8}(4\log\lambda_{j+2})^3$. Suppose $\tau_1\le1/4$, $4\tau_{j+1}\le\tau_j$, $t_1=0$, and $t_{j+1}-t_j\le\tau_j$. With $S_0=1$ and $S_j=t_j+2\tau_j$, the formal statement proves $S_{j+1}<S_j$ for every $j\ge0$. It does not need activation times to be increasing. In the construction, where all times are nonnegative, this ensures $[0,S_j]\subset[0,S_{j-1}]$, so the preceding velocity is available throughout the new endpoint problem. Existence or regularity of that velocity is not part of this estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_exists: Assume an integer $b\ge1$, a real initial frequency $N\ge1$, and $\mathcal B(1)\le N$. The formal theorem constructs integer orders $q_j$ and real frequencies $\lambda_j$ with $q_1=1$, $\lambda_0=N$, $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{320b(q_j+1)}$, and $q_{j+1}=\max\{1\le s\le q_j+1:\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}\}$ for $j\ge1$. No positivity, monotonicity or logarithmic lower bound for the entire threshold function is assumed. The result establishes existence of these sequences only. It does not by itself prove $q_j\to\infty$, the gain bound (1.15), or any Euler construction; those require further hypotheses and results.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_frequency_t: Let $b\ge1$ be an integer, let $\lambda_0=N>1$, and assume $\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j^{320b(q_{j+1}+1)}$ for a sequence of nonnegative integers $q_j$. The formal statement proves $\lambda_j\to\infty$. It uses only the initial frequency and this recurrence: no threshold function or maximal-order rule is needed. Every exponent is an integer at least two, so the proof obtains a growing lower bound from powers of $N$. This supplies the frequency-growth step in Appendix C. It does not establish $q_j\to\infty$, which requires the separate rule for selecting the orders.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_fullOrder_p: Let $\mu\ge1$, let $b\ge1$, $q,P\ge0$ be integers, and suppose a real constant $C$ satisfies $C\le\mu$. Set $K=320b(q+1)$ and $\lambda=\mu^K$. Then $C\mu^{5(P+1)+1}\le\lambda^{P+2}$. This is the scalar comparison used after the Bernstein estimate for the parent velocity at order $P$. The statement does not itself bound a velocity norm and does not require $P$ to be the expansion depth $6K_{j+1}$. The integer exponents are ordinary powers; positivity of $\mu$ follows from $\mu\ge1$.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_fullOrder_w: For real $\mu\ge1$, integers $b\ge1$, $q,P\ge0$, and $C\le\mu$, set $\mathsf D=\mu^9$ and $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q+1)}$. The formal statement proves $C\mathsf D^{b(P+2)}\le\lambda^{(P+2)/32}$. The right side is a real power of a positive frequency; the derivative order $P$ and coefficient exponent $b$ are integers. In §7.2 this is applied to the fixed-order constant in the wave estimate, once the threshold gives $C\le\mu$. It is a numerical absorption estimate, not a bound for the oscillatory field or its derivatives by itself.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_halfLength_: Let $b\ge1$ be an integer, $K(s)=320b(s+1)$, $q_1=1$, $\lambda_0\ge\mathcal B(1)$, and $\lambda_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{K(q_j)}$. Suppose $q_{j+1}$ is the largest integer $1\le s\le q_j+1$ with $\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}$, and $\mathcal B(s)>0$, $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$ for $s\ge1$. There is an absolute threshold for $\lambda_0$ above which, at every $j\ge1$, $0<\tau_j\le\lambda_{j-1}^{-1/16}$ and $4\tau_{j+1}\le\tau_j$, where $\tau_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{-1/8}(4\log\lambda_{j+2})^3$. Unlike §1.5, this statement does not assume that $\mathcal B$ is nondecreasing or bounds analytic constants. Its internal index $i$ denotes $\tau_{i+1}$.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_log_bound: Write $K(q)=320b(q+1)$, assume $\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j^{K(q_{j+1})}$ and $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$. At an index $i$, suppose $q_{i+1}\le q_{i+2}$, $q_{i+3}\le q_{i+2}+1$, $\mathcal B(q_{i+2})>0$, $4K(q_{i+2}+1)^3\le\log\mathcal B(q_{i+2})$, and $\mathcal B(q_{i+2})\le\lambda_i$. The formal statement proves $L_{i+2}\le(\log\lambda_i)^2$. Setting $j=i+1$ gives (1.15) and the conclusion of Appendix C. The inequalities bounding the three exponents occur inside the proof; the declaration itself states the final gain bound. No full admissibility condition on the threshold function is assumed beyond the listed local inequalities.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_lowOrder_me: Let $\mu\ge1$, let $b\ge1$ and $m,q\ge0$ be integers with $m\le q$, and suppose $C\le\mu$. For $\mathsf D=\mu^9$ and $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q+1)}$, the formal theorem gives $C\mathsf D^{b(m+2)}\le\lambda^{1/16}$. This is the coefficient bound used for the mean part of the velocity increment through order $q_j$. It assumes the relevant fixed-order constant has already been bounded by the parent frequency. It does not estimate the mean field itself, and it states the final frequency power rather than the intervening bound by $\mu^{10b(m+2)}$.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_order_advan: Let $q_{\rm next}$ be the largest integer $s$ with $1\le s\le q+1$ and $\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{\rm prev}$. The formal statement proves $q_{\rm next}=q+1$ if and only if $\mathcal B(q+1)\le\lambda_{\rm prev}$. It assumes that this largest integer exists; it does not prove nonemptiness of the admissible set. To conclude that the order otherwise stays equal to $q$, one must also know that $q$ is admissible. Appendix C establishes that fact from the previous step. Thus this declaration gives the exact threshold for an increase, while the separate monotonicity estimate gives the other alternative.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_order_steps: Assume $q_1=1$, $\mathcal B(1)\le\lambda_0$, a nondecreasing frequency sequence, and the rule $q_{j+1}=\max\{1\le s\le q_j+1:\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}\}$ for every $j\ge1$. The formal statement proves $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$. Its proof shows that the current order remains admissible, first from the initial condition and then from the preceding maximum and frequency monotonicity. The displayed conclusion is the pair of order inequalities, not a separate admissibility assertion. The exact criterion deciding between equality and increase is proved in the neighboring threshold result.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_order_tends: Let $q_1=1$, $\mathcal B(1)\le\lambda_0$, and suppose the real frequency sequence is nondecreasing and tends to infinity. At each step choose $q_{j+1}$ as the largest integer $s$ with $1\le s\le q_j+1$ and $\mathcal B(s)\le\lambda_{j-1}$. The formal theorem proves $q_j\to\infty$: every fixed derivative order is eventually retained. The threshold may grow arbitrarily quickly and need not be monotone, because each individual value is finite and is eventually exceeded. This generalizes the corresponding assertion in §1.5. The theorem assumes frequency divergence; it does not derive that divergence from a recurrence.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_residual_bu: Let $\lambda\ge2$, and let $b\ge1$ and $q_+\ge0$ be integers. Define $\lambda_+=\lambda^{320b(q_++1)}$. Then $2\lambda^{2+1/16}\lambda_+^{-4}\le\lambda_+^{-7/2}$. This is exactly the last numerical inequality in (7.11), with $\lambda_+=\lambda_{j+1}$. It has no velocity, pressure or residual among its data. To deduce the estimate for $R_V$, one must first prove $\|R_V\|_{C_tC^{1,1/2}}\le2\lambda^{2+1/16}\lambda_+^{-4}$ from the expansion and switching errors. All fractional powers here have positive bases.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_residual_ex: Let $\lambda\ge0$, let $b,q_+\ge0$ be integers, and put $K_+=320b(q_++1)$ and $P=6K_+$. The formal statement proves $\lambda^{-2P/3}=(\lambda^{K_+})^{-4}$. In the induction, $b\ge1$ and $\lambda>1$, so $\lambda^{K_+}=\lambda_{j+1}$ and this is the remainder identity used after (7.2). The formal theorem also permits $\lambda=0$ and $b=0$: powers at zero follow the formal convention $0^0=1$ and $0^r=0$ for nonzero real $r$. Those extra cases are not assertions about zero-frequency waves and are unused in the construction.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_step_consta: Let $b\ge1$ and $q\ge0$ be integers, let $\mu\ge1$, and suppose $A\le\mu$. With $\mathsf D=\mu^9$ and $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q+1)}$, the formal statement gives $A\mathsf D^b\le\mu^{10b}\le\lambda^{1/32}$ and $(A\mathsf D^b)\mu\le\lambda^{1/16}$. Taking $A=\mathcal B(q_{j+1})$ supplies (7.8) once the recurrence has given $A\le\mu$. The last bound also supplies the extra factor needed for the residual estimate. These are scalar inequalities; the theorem does not itself select the threshold or show that it bounds a particular analytic constant.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_tail_absorp: Let $\mu\ge2$ and let $b\ge1$, $q,q_+\ge0$ be integers. Put $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q+1)}$, $K_+=320b(q_++1)$, $P=6K_+$ and $\lambda_+=\lambda^{K_+}$. Then $9\mu\lambda^{5(2-P)+4(P+1)}\le\lambda_+^{-5}$. In particular, $2-P$ is subtraction of real numbers in this exponent, so it may be negative; it is not truncated to zero. The formal statement supplies the numerical absorption in (7.12). It does not supply the preceding estimate for the actual cutoff error $\varepsilon_\Lambda$, and it does not require a relation between $q$ and $q_+$.
notes.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_three_log_s: Let $K(q)=320b(q+1)$, suppose $\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j^{K(q_{j+1})}$, and put $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$. The formal identity is $L_{i+2}=4K(q_{i+1})K(q_{i+2})K(q_{i+3})\log\lambda_i$. With $j=i+1$ this is the three-step expansion displayed in Appendix C. The recurrence uses nonnegative integer exponents. The formal logarithm equals $\log|x|$ for $x\ne0$ and is assigned zero at $x=0$. The identity assumes no positivity; the paper applies it only to frequencies greater than one. No threshold bound or order monotonicity is needed for this identity, and no gain inequality is concluded here.
notes.TorusEuler.frozenSymbol: For bounded operators $r,B$ on a real Hilbert space, define $A=rBr+I-r$. In Appendix A.1, $r=r(n)$ is the orthogonal projection for a Fourier mode and $B=B(a_0)$ is the coefficient frozen at a label. On the range of a projection, $A$ acts as the projected coefficient; on its kernel, $A$ is the identity. The formula itself allows arbitrary $r,B$. Idempotence, orthogonality and coercivity are separate assumptions used to justify this decomposition and to obtain invertibility.
notes.TorusEuler.frozenSymbol_apply_of_proj_eq: If bounded operators $r,B$ and a vector $v$ satisfy $rv=0$, then $(rBr+I-r)v=v$. This algebraic fact does not require $r$ to be an orthogonal projection or $B$ to be coercive. For the orthogonal Fourier projection in Lemma A.2, its kernel is the orthogonal complement of its range, so the statement proves the paper's assertion that the extended frozen coefficient acts as the identity on that complement.
notes.TorusEuler.frozenSymbol_coercive: Let $r$ be an orthogonal projection and assume $\langle Bv,v\rangle\ge\mu\|v\|^2$ for every $v$ in its range. Then $A=rBr+I-r$ satisfies $\langle Av,v\rangle\ge\min(1,\mu)\|v\|^2$ for every vector in the real Hilbert space. Positivity of $\mu$ is not required for this inequality, but it is needed for the inverse argument. This gives the final real lower bound in Appendix A.1; the displayed complex real-part inequality and its intermediate two-term bound require the separate complexification argument.
notes.TorusEuler.gradientIntegral_eq_top_of_cu: For a velocity field $u$, if $\int_0^T\|\operatorname{curl}u(t)\|_\infty\,dt=\infty$, then $\int_0^T\|\nabla u(t)\|_\infty\,dt=\infty$. The formal statement uses nonnegative Lebesgue integrals on $[0,T)$ and essential suprema on the centred unit cell; the matrix norm is the operator norm. The deduction uses the fixed linear inequality $\|\operatorname{curl}v\|_\infty\le C\|\nabla v\|_\infty$, so no Euler equation or continuation criterion is required.
